mcqs.question: What is a subclass's real dependency surface on its base class, according to the fragile base class argument?
options: Only the methods the subclass explicitly overrides
The base class's declared contract plus every implementation detail the subclass happens to rely on, even though only the contract was ever promised
Only the private fields of the base class
Nothing beyond the base class's constructor signature
mcqs.explanation: The fragile base class problem is exactly that a subclass ends up depending on undocumented internals — call order, side effects — in addition to the declared contract, even though it never agreed to depend on those internals. Overridden methods alone, private fields alone, or the constructor signature alone all understate the real surface.

mcqs.question: In the diagram of a base class's declared contract versus its actual dependency surface, what does the larger dashed region represent?
options: The set of unit tests that currently pass for the base class
The subset of methods marked as deprecated
The classes that currently extend this base class
Everything a subclass ends up depending on in practice, including undocumented call order and side effects, beyond just the declared public contract
mcqs.explanation: The dashed region captures the full real dependency surface — declared contract plus undocumented internals a subclass happens to rely on — which is the core of the fragile base class problem. It isn't about test coverage, deprecation status, or which classes currently extend the base.

mcqs.question: If `protected` visibility is a legitimate, useful tool, what specifically causes the fragile base class problem?
options: Undeclared coupling — behavior a subclass depends on that was never marked as part of any contract, protected or otherwise, not the existence of `protected` itself
The use of `protected` fields at all, which should always be avoided
The fact that subclasses exist in a different file than their base class
Using more than one level of inheritance depth
mcqs.explanation: `protected` is a real, narrower promise than `public` and is fine when used deliberately for genuine extension points — the actual leak is behavior a subclass depends on that was never documented as part of any contract at all. File location and inheritance depth aren't the mechanism here, and `protected` itself isn't inherently the problem.

mcqs.question: Why is "inheritance leaks encapsulation, so never use it" considered an overcorrection?
options: Because inheritance never actually leaks encapsulation in any case
Because composition has exactly the same risk as inheritance, so switching doesn't help at all

It overcorrects past a narrower claim — inheritance modeling a genuine, stable relationship with a well-documented, frozen contract is a legitimate tool; the real fix is disciplined contracts, not blanket avoidance
Because avoiding inheritance always makes code slower
mcqs.explanation: The actual claim is narrower and more useful than a blanket ban — the risk is real, but it's addressed by making contracts explicit (final methods, documented hooks) rather than avoiding inheritance entirely, which throws away a legitimate tool for genuine is-a relationships. Inheritance can leak encapsulation, composition meaningfully reduces that specific risk, and this isn't a performance argument.
